analysis.one_liner: Gives federal grants to states and cities that guarantee free lawyers to low-income tenants facing eviction.
analysis.headline: The Eviction Right to Counsel Act of 2024 died in committee with no hearing, no vote, and not a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a federal fund of $100 million a year for five years. States, cities, and tribal governments could get grants if they pass a law giving free, full legal representation to tenants earning up to 200% of the poverty line who are facing eviction or loss of a housing subsidy. Federal money would flow preferentially to places that also limit no-fault evictions, require 30 days' notice, set up eviction diversion programs, or provide emergency rental assistance.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income tenants — those at or below 200% of the federal poverty line — facing eviction from their primary residence or termination of a housing subsidy. They would get a lawyer at no cost, which in practice means fewer evictions and more time to negotiate or relocate. The bill would also fund recruitment and training of attorneys who take these cases, and would reward states and cities that add tenant protections like just-cause eviction rules and 30-day notice requirements. Landlord-tenant courts, currently clogged with unrepresented defendants, could process cases more fairly.

how_it_helps.text: Creates an Eviction Right to Counsel Fund with $100 million per year for fiscal years 2025 through 2029, to be run by the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development.

States, local governments, and tribal governments qualify for grants only if they enact legislation providing full legal representation, at no cost, to every tenant at or below 200% of the federal poverty line in an eviction or subsidy-termination case.

Prioritizes grant money for jurisdictions that also limit no-fault evictions, require at least 30 days' written notice before eviction, establish eviction diversion programs, or provide emergency rental assistance, and for recipients who use funds to recruit and train eviction defense attorneys.
The right applies not just to evictions but to termination of a housing subsidy, protecting tenants from losing the assistance that keeps housing affordable.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund $100 million a year for five years in appropriations. Landlords would also bear indirect costs: tenants with lawyers fight evictions more effectively, and the priority rules reward jurisdictions that restrict no-fault evictions and require 30 days' notice, which can make removing a tenant slower and more expensive. Some of that cost could show up in rents over time.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes $100 million per year in new federal spending for five years, a cost to taxpayers with no dedicated funding source identified in the bill.

No tenant gets a lawyer directly from this bill: the federal money only reaches tenants after their own state, city, or tribal government first passes right-to-counsel legislation, so coverage would be uneven and depend entirely on local action.
Eligibility stops at 200% of the federal poverty line, so many tenants just above that line — including many working households — would still face eviction court alone.
By making evictions slower and costlier for landlords, the bill could reduce rental supply or raise rents in some markets, a cost that could land partly on tenants themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest in scale: $100 million a year is a small fraction of what eviction defense would cost nationwide, and the money only flows where local governments already act, which limits both reach and waste. The design is defensible — it conditions federal money on local commitment and rewards stronger tenant protections — but a low-income tenant's right to a lawyer would depend on where they live, and the bill died before any of this could be tested. The main cost is the $100 million annual appropriation and some friction for landlords that could feed into rents.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final weeks of the session, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, and the Congress ended before the committee did anything with it.

narrative.text: Rep. Summer Lee introduced the bill on December 19, 2024, during the final days of the 118th Congress.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.

The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced; the committee held no hearing, reported no bill, and no vote was ever taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
Because the bill was not passed by both chambers, it expired when the Congress ended and would have to be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and their industry groups are better off, since no federal incentives for right-to-counsel laws or eviction restrictions ever took effect. Defense attorneys and legal aid organizations gained nothing either — the promised $500 million in funding never materialized. Tenants are exactly where they started.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on December 19, 2024 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.what_they_did: None signed on as cosponsors, leaving the bill with no demonstrated support in the chamber.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got far enough for a party split to show: a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and no vote ever taken.

industries.note: Tenants with lawyers contest evictions far more effectively, and the bill steers federal money toward jurisdictions that limit no-fault evictions and require 30 days' notice, making removals slower and costlier. The bill's whole purpose was to shift leverage in eviction court from landlords to tenants, which is why landlord interests had no reason to support it.

industries.industry: Legal aid and eviction defense attorneys
industries.note: The bill would fund recruitment and training of attorneys to represent tenants in eviction and subsidy-termination cases, expanding paid work for the eviction defense bar and legal aid organizations. Their gain runs alongside the tenant's gain.
